amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-9-0129 allowing lawful cannabis dispensaries to modify operations to include medical cannabis without triggering Section 17-9-0129.1
amendments.summary: A lawfully established adult-use cannabis dispensary may add medical cannabis dispensary operations without special use or Type I map amendment or planned development review (new §17-9-0129 item 8). Any physical expansion of the use, structures or zoning lot still triggers that review.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Chapter 17-3 by adding Section 17-3-0600 regarding transient-oriented development (TOD) streets
amendments.summary: Adds §17-3-0600, transit-oriented development (TOD) streets: N Ravenswood Ave from Irving Park Rd to Lawrence Ave (4001–4799 N) and N Western Ave from Addison St to Ainslie St (3600–4859 N). Eight uses are prohibited on lots abutting a TOD street (strip centers, drive-through facilities, vehicle sales and service with outdoor storage, gas stations, car washes, residential storage warehouses, electronic data storage centers, motor vehicle repair shops). A rezoning of abutting property must be to a B or C1 district with a FAR of at least 3 (applications complete and pending before the effective date follow the old rules unless the applicant opts in). It also ends the §17-3-0308(2) pedestrian-street exceptions on a TOD segment and adds a definition at §17-17-02177.5. Effective on passage.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-7-1506 exempting adaptive reuse or rehabilitated strip centers from prohibitions within Milwaukee Avenue Special Character Overlay District
amendments.summary: Adds an exception to the Milwaukee Avenue Special Character Overlay District's ban on strip centers (§17-7-1506): a strip center is allowed in the case of adaptive reuse or rehabilitation of an existing building. The other four prohibited uses are unchanged.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-9-0111.5 to include religious assembly in non-accessory parking restrictions in RT4 and higher zoning districts
amendments.summary: Allows non-accessory parking on religious assembly grounds currently devoted to accessory parking, in RT4 and higher R districts, up to eight spaces and only when no religious services are being held (new §17-9-0111.5-B; the school rule is §17-9-0111.5-A).

amendments.title: De-designation of segments of W Lawrence Ave right-of-way on Map No. 13-I as pedestrian street and amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-3-0503-D modifying pedestrian streets on portions of W Lawrence Ave - App No. A-9135
amendments.summary: Removes the pedestrian-street designation from W Lawrence Ave between Whipple St and Albany Ave (3032–3042 W; common address 3034–3042), splitting the Sacramento–Central Park row into Sacramento–Whipple (3000–3032 W) and Albany–Central Park (3042–3600 W).

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-6-0403-F to permit by right residential storage warehouses in Planned Manufacturing District 4B
amendments.summary: Changes the Residential Storage Warehouse row of the §17-6-0403-F use table: PMD 4B becomes special use (S). The ordinance's title says 'by right', but the substitute that passed enters S for that district.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-6-0403 to establish size restrictions for participant sports and recreation use as permitted by right in planned manufacturing districts
amendments.summary: Adds a supplemental standard (§17-6-0403-G.18): participant sports and recreation uses in PMDs may not exceed 9,000 sq ft, except in PMD 2, 3, 4A, 5, 7A, 7B, 8A, 8B, 10, 11B and 14, and in PMD 4B when approved as a special use. It also edits that use-table row's PMD 4B entry (the strike-through and underline are hard to read on the scan).

amendments.title: Designation of areas on Map Nos. 7-F, 7-G, 9-F, and 9-G as pedestrian retail streets and amendment of municipal code Section 17-3-0503-D establishing pedestrian streets and retail streets on portion of W Belmont Ave
amendments.summary: Designates W Belmont Ave from N Cambridge Ave (531 W) to N Southport Ave (1400 W) a pedestrian retail street. The listed segment used to start at Halsted (800 W), so 531–800 W is new. The §17-3-0504 pedestrian-street standards apply to pedestrian retail streets too.

amendments.title: Designation of areas on Map Nos.5-F, 7-F, 7-G, and 9-G as pedestrian retail streets and amendment of municipal code Section 17-3-0503-D establishing pedestrian streets and retail streets on portion of N Clark St

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-9-0109A to require special use approval for all new gas stations and for additions to existing gas stations that would add seven or more electric vehicle supply chargers
amendments.summary: Adds a trigger to §17-9-0109-A: an addition to an existing gas station that adds 7 or more electric vehicle supply equipment chargers needs special use approval, like 2 or more new pumps. **Short answer: No — not by right at 443 W Wrightwood Ave.**

This parcel (PIN 14-28-318-057-0000, matched via Cook County Address Points) is zoned **RM-6** — a high-density residential multi-unit district [4]. Restaurants are an **Eating and Drinking Establishment** use [5], and that use category simply does not appear in the RM residential use table [4]. The RM-6 district allows detached houses, two-flats, townhouses, multi-unit buildings, parks, schools, and community centers — no commercial food service uses.

For comparison, restaurants are allowed by right in B3, C1, C2, and C3 commercial districts [2], and limited restaurants (no full service) are permitted in B1 and B2 as well [2]. This lot is residential-zoned, so none of those commercial permissions apply here.

**To put a restaurant at this address you would need a rezoning** — typically to a B or C district — which requires a map amendment and aldermanic notice [§17-13-0300]. That is a discretionary approval this analysis cannot predict.

A few additional context points:
- The parcel is within the **Lakefront Protection District** and on the **National Register's Lakeview Historic District**, which could add further review layers to any rezoning application.
- The parcel is also in an **Affordable Requirements Ordinance zone**, so a rezoning to a residential-commercial mixed use would trigger ARO obligations. Lincoln Park already has 5 ARO-linked affordable housing projects totaling 186 units in the community area.
- Lincoln Park's food scene is active: 714 food inspections on record in the community area, with a 17.6% fail rate [data:food_inspections], suggesting a competitive and well-regulated dining environment.

The Municipal Code text used here is current through the Council Journal of June 17, 2026; City Council passed 10 amendments to Title 17 since then, though none of those listed appear to change RM-district restaurant permissions.

Title 10 — STREETS, PUBLIC WAYS, PARKS, AIRPORTS AND HARBORS
Chapter 10-28 — STRUCTURES ON AND UNDER PUBLIC WAYS
Article XII — SIDEWALK CAFES (10-28-800 et seq.)
§ 10-28-800 — Definitions

Wherever used in this article, unless the context clearly indicates otherwise:

(A) " Alcoholic beverages " means and includes alcohol, spirits, wine and beer.

(B) " Commissioner " means the commissioner of business affairs and consumer protection."

(C) " Department " means the department of business affairs and consumer protection of the City of Chicago.

(D) " Food " means any raw, cooked or processed edible substance or ingredient, used or intended for use in whole or in part for human consumption, and shall include nonalcoholic beverages allowed to be sold in accordance with this article, but shall not include alcoholic beverages.

(E) " Indoor retail market " means any building under common ownership or management containing a group of commercial establishments which offer a variety of retail, restaurant or service uses and in which at least two of the establishments hold a valid retail food establishment license.

(F) " Person " has the meaning ascribed to the term in Section 1-4-090(e) of the code.

(G) " Sidewalk café " means a portion of an immobile retail food establishment or an indoor retail market located on a public right-of-way, whether directly adjacent to, or in close proximity to, the retail food establishment or an indoor retail market .

Title 4 — BUSINESSES, OCCUPATIONS AND CONSUMER PROTECTION
Chapter 4-8 — FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS*
§ 4-8-010 — Definitions
(part 13 of 19)

"Retail food establishment" means any building, room, stand, enclosure, place or establishment occupied and used as a place of business for the purpose of serving, storing, selling, offering for sale or keeping with the intention of selling or distributing at retail any article of food, drink, confection or condiment, ultimately used for or intended to be used for human consumption. The term shall include, but not be limited to: restaurants, coffee shops, cafeterias, short order cafes, luncheonettes, grills, tearooms, sandwich shops, soda fountains, taverns, bars, cocktail lounges, nightclubs, industrial feeding establishments, take-out establishments, private institutions or organizations routinely serving food, catering kitchens, commissaries or any other eating or drinking establishment or operation, the automatic food-vending machine business, coffee cart vendors, candy manufacturers, confectioneries, fish markets, fruit and vegetable markets, grocery stores, meat markets, nut stores, dressed poultry markets or retail bakeries, bakery outlets or any similar place.

"Rules of the Department of Health" means rules adopted by the Commissioner or the Board of Health, as authorized in this Code, for the proper administration or enforcement of the provisions of this Code pertaining to the regulation of food establishments, including Chapters 4-8, 7-38, 7-40, and 7-42.

"Sanitized" means effective bactericidal treatment of clean surfaces of equipment and utensils by a process which has been approved by the Department of Health as being effective in destroying microorganisms, including pathogens.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-9-0129 allowing lawful cannabis dispensaries to modify operations to include medical cannabis without triggering Section 17-9-0129.1
amendments.summary: A lawfully established adult-use cannabis dispensary may add medical cannabis dispensary operations without special use or Type I map amendment or planned development review (new §17-9-0129 item 8). Any physical expansion of the use, structures or zoning lot still triggers that review.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Chapter 17-3 by adding Section 17-3-0600 regarding transient-oriented development (TOD) streets
amendments.summary: Adds §17-3-0600, transit-oriented development (TOD) streets: N Ravenswood Ave from Irving Park Rd to Lawrence Ave (4001–4799 N) and N Western Ave from Addison St to Ainslie St (3600–4859 N). Eight uses are prohibited on lots abutting a TOD street (strip centers, drive-through facilities, vehicle sales and service with outdoor storage, gas stations, car washes, residential storage warehouses, electronic data storage centers, motor vehicle repair shops). A rezoning of abutting property must be to a B or C1 district with a FAR of at least 3 (applications complete and pending before the effective date follow the old rules unless the applicant opts in). It also ends the §17-3-0308(2) pedestrian-street exceptions on a TOD segment and adds a definition at §17-17-02177.5. Effective on passage.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-7-1506 exempting adaptive reuse or rehabilitated strip centers from prohibitions within Milwaukee Avenue Special Character Overlay District
amendments.summary: Adds an exception to the Milwaukee Avenue Special Character Overlay District's ban on strip centers (§17-7-1506): a strip center is allowed in the case of adaptive reuse or rehabilitation of an existing building. The other four prohibited uses are unchanged.

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-9-0111.5 to include religious assembly in non-accessory parking restrictions in RT4 and higher zoning districts
amendments.summary: Allows non-accessory parking on religious assembly grounds currently devoted to accessory parking, in RT4 and higher R districts, up to eight spaces and only when no religious services are being held (new §17-9-0111.5-B; the school rule is §17-9-0111.5-A).

amendments.title: Amendment of Municipal Code Section 17-6-0403 to establish size restrictions for participant sports and recreation use as permitted by right in planned manufacturing districts

**Same answer, unfortunately — a coffee shop is also not permitted by right at 443 W Wrightwood Ave.**

A coffee shop falls under the **Eating and Drinking Establishment** use category [4] (or **Food and Beverage Retail Sales** if it operates purely as a retail counter [4]). Neither use appears in the RM-6 residential use table [4]. The RM-6 district is limited to residential uses — detached houses, two-flats, townhouses, multi-unit buildings, parks, schools, and community centers — with no commercial food or beverage uses permitted [4].

The same path applies as with a full restaurant: **you would need a rezoning to a B or C district** to permit an eating/drinking establishment or food retail use by right [2]. That requires a map amendment with aldermanic notice [§17-13-0300] — a discretionary process this analysis cannot predict.

A few nuances worth noting:
- **Small coffee retail** (packaged beans, no seating) might theoretically be argued as incidental accessory use, but RM-6 does not contemplate commercial accessory uses of this type, and the safer read is that it is prohibited.
- **Lincoln Park's commercial landscape** is active — 435 Retail Food Establishment licenses and 160 "Consumption on Premises" licenses are already active in the community area [data:business] — so there is clearly demand, but this parcel's zoning keeps commercial uses out regardless.
- The **Lakefront Protection District** and **Lakeview Historic District** overlays would add review layers to any rezoning application here.

**Short answer: A tavern is not permitted by right at 2200 W Chicago Ave — it requires a Special Use approval.**

---

## Zoning

This parcel is zoned **B2-3** (Neighborhood Mixed-Use) [1], matched via Cook County Assessor's Parcel Addresses (PIN 17063290360000). Under [1], a **tavern** in a B2 district is listed as **"S" — Special Use** — meaning you cannot open one simply by pulling a building permit. You must apply to the Zoning Board of Appeals for a special use authorization before a license can issue.

By contrast, a **Restaurant, Limited** (counter service, takeout) or **Restaurant, General** (full sit-down) would be **permitted by right ("P")** in a B3, C1, or C2 district [1], but B2 does not permit a general restaurant by right either — only a limited restaurant is permitted by right in B2 [1]. If your concept is primarily a tavern (liquor-focused, with food incidental), the Special Use path applies.

---

## What "Special Use" Means in Practice

A Special Use requires:
- Filing an application with the Zoning Board of Appeals (§17-13-0900)
- A public hearing
- Aldermanic notification (§17-13-0300)
- A finding that the use meets the general and specific criteria in the code

Approval is discretionary — this analysis cannot predict the outcome.

---

## Other Site Factors

- **Flood zone:** FEMA Zone X (area of minimal flood hazard) — no flood insurance requirement here.
- **Special Service Area:** This parcel is within the **West Town-2014** Special Service Area, which funds enhanced streetscaping and business support services in the corridor.
- **ARO zone:** Any new residential development above the bar would trigger Affordable Requirements Ordinance obligations.
- **ADU:** Coach houses and conversion units are permitted by right in this district (§17-7-0573, §17-7-0574) — relevant if you plan a mixed-use build.
- **SBIF grants:** West Town has an active Small Business Improvement Fund program — 15 recent projects totaling over $1 million [data:business] in grants for façade and interior work. A bar buildout could potentially qualify.

---

## Code Currency Note

The Municipal Code text cited here runs through the Council Journal of June 17, 2026. City Council has passed 10 Title 17 amendments since then (as of November 2, 2026), including a new **Transient-Oriented Development Streets** section (SO2026-0025391, passed October 14, 2026) that added §17-3-0600 to Chapter 17-3. That amendment is not in the retrieved code text; if Chicago Ave is designated a TOD street under it, use standards could differ — verify with the Zoning Administrator.

---

**How to verify:** Confirm the Special Use requirement at §17-3-0200 and §17-13-0900; request a Zoning Verification Letter from the Office of the Zoning Administrator ($150, up to 30 days). For the special use process, contact the Zoning Board of Appeals directly.

**In Chicago's residential zoning districts, restaurants are generally not permitted.** The use tables for residential districts follow a strict framework: only uses explicitly listed with a "P" (permitted by-right), "S" (special use), or "PD" (planned development) designation are allowed — everything else is expressly prohibited [2].

Under [2], uses identified with a "–" are expressly prohibited, and **uses not listed in the table at all are also prohibited**. Restaurants (a retail food and beverage use) are a commercial use category, not a residential one, so they do not appear as permitted or special uses in the residential use table.

**Key distinctions to keep in mind:**

- **Business and Commercial districts (B1, B2, B3, C1, C2, C3)** are where restaurants and food service establishments are typically allowed [1] — not in R-zoned residential districts.
- **Manufacturing districts (M1, M2, M3)** have their own separate use framework [3], also distinct from residential.
- **Live/work arrangements** in certain districts can combine residential and commercial activity, but those units must have pedestrian-oriented frontage, publicly display the commercial space, and meet strict integration requirements [5] — and even then, they apply in specific non-residential or mixed-use districts, not standard residential zones.

**How to verify:** The full residential use table is in §17-2-0207. If you have a specific residential district (e.g., RS-3, RT-4, RM-5), that table will show every permitted and special use for that district. The special use procedures, if a creative interpretation were ever pursued, are governed by §17-13-0900.

Note: 10 Zoning Ordinance amendments have passed since the Council Journal of June 17, 2026 (the basis of the code text above), so a later amendment could potentially affect specific use categories — confirm with the Department of Planning and Development.

The M2-3 (Light Industry) district's use table does not include residential uses. As the zoning table makes clear, housing is simply not in the M-district use table, and unlisted uses are prohibited under [1]. A rezoning or Planned Development (§17-5-0204) would be required to add residential use to this site.

A few additional points worth knowing:

- **No path to residential by right or special use.** Unlike some B and C districts where residential above ground-floor commercial is a standard option, M districts have no residential row in the use table at all — there is nothing to trigger even a special use application.
- **A rezoning is the only route.** You'd need a map amendment to a business, commercial, or residential district, which is a discretionary approval requiring aldermanic notice and City Council action [2]. Given the parcel's industrial context, that is not straightforward.
- **Mixed-use restaurant + residential would require a different district entirely.** A B2 or C1 district, for example, allows both ground-floor restaurant use and upper-floor residential. That would require a full rezoning.
- **No ADU option either.** This parcel is not in an ADU-eligible area, so accessory dwelling units (coach houses or conversion units) are also not available here.

The parcel's lot area is approximately 39,512 sq ft (our calculation) across a complex of six PIN parcels, so there is real scale to work with — but unlocking residential use means starting with a rezoning conversation with the alderman's office.

**No — a new gas station cannot be opened at 368 W Chicago Ave under current rules.**

There are two independent bars:

**1. C2-5 zoning prohibits new gas stations**
This parcel is zoned C2-5 (Motor Vehicle-Related Commercial), matched to PIN 17044360170000 via Cook County Address Points. The C2-5 use table expressly prohibits new gas stations [4] — the zone definition in context confirms "no new gas stations (§17-3-0207)" as a named exclusion from the otherwise very broad C2-5 commercial use list.

**2. A citywide amendment has tightened gas station rules further**
The Municipal Code text here is current through the Council Journal of June 17, 2026. City Council passed an amendment on July 15, 2026 (O2026-0025429) requiring special use approval for **all** new gas stations citywide and for additions to existing stations that would add seven or more EV chargers. That amendment is not yet codified in the text you can read, but it is in effect. So even if the base zoning were permissive, a new gas station would still require a special use hearing — and the C2-5 prohibition means it could not be approved in this district regardless.

**Other relevant factors at this site:**
- The parcel is in an **Affordable Requirements Ordinance zone** and a **CTA Transit-Oriented Development area**. Under TOD rules, the minimum parking requirement can be reduced by up to 100% [§17-10-0102-B], but that parking relief does not change the use prohibition on gas stations.
- The parcel is within **Chicago Enterprise Zone 4**, which offers certain tax incentives for eligible businesses — but gas stations are not an eligible use here regardless.
- The site is in FEMA Flood Zone X (minimal flood hazard), so there are no flood-related constraints beyond the zoning issue.

**A car wash faces the same hard prohibition as a gas station at this address — it cannot be opened at 368 W Chicago Ave.**

Here's why:

**C2-5 zoning: car washes are prohibited**
The C2-5 district [2] is intentionally broad — it allows "nearly any type of business, service or commercial use" — but the zone definition in context explicitly excludes new gas stations (§17-3-0207), and car washes fall under the Vehicle Sales and Service use category [1], which is separately regulated. More critically:

**Pedestrian street rule doesn't apply here, but a broader prohibition does**
Although this parcel is **not** on a designated pedestrian street (confirmed in the regulatory data), [4] expressly lists car washes among the uses prohibited on pedestrian-street lots. That said, the operative bar here comes from the C2-5 use table itself under §17-3-0207, which the zone definition confirms prohibits car washes alongside gas stations.

**Key factors to note:**
- **TOD overlay**: The parcel is in a CTA Transit-Oriented Development area, meaning parking minimums can be reduced by up to 100% [§17-10-0102-B] — but parking relief does not change the use prohibition on a car wash.
- **ARO zone**: The Affordable Requirements Ordinance zone applies if any residential component is added, but is irrelevant to a car wash use.
- **Chicago Enterprise Zone 4**: Tax incentives are available here, but only for eligible uses — a car wash is not an eligible use regardless.
- **Vehicle Storage and Towing** (indoor) is listed as a permitted use in C2 [1], so not all vehicle-related uses are banned — but a car wash is specifically excluded.

**How to verify:** §17-3-0207 (C2-5 use table, car wash row) and [4] (§17-3-0504-H for pedestrian street context). CHICAGO MUNICIPAL CODE
Title 17 — CHICAGO ZONING ORDINANCE
Chapter 17-2 — RESIDENTIAL DISTRICTS
§ 17-2-0100 — District descriptions
(part 1 of 3)

17-2-0101 Generally. The "R", residential districts are intended to create, maintain and promote a variety of housing opportunities for individual households and to maintain the desired physical character of the city's existing neighborhoods. While the districts primarily accommodate residential use types, nonresidential uses that are compatible with residential neighborhoods are also allowed.

17-2-0102 RS, Residential Single-Unit (Detached House) Districts. The primary purpose of the RS districts is to accommodate the development of detached houses on individual lots . It is intended that RS zoning be applied in areas where the land-use pattern is characterized predominately by detached houses on individual lots or where such a land use pattern is desired in the future. The Zoning Ordinance includes three RS districts – RS1, RS2 and RS3 – which are differentiated primarily on the basis of minimum lot area requirements and floor area ratios .

17-2-0103 RT, Residential Two-Flat, Townhouse and Multi-Unit Districts. The primary purpose of the RT districts is to accommodate detached houses, two-flats , townhouses and low-density, multi-unit residential buildings at a density and building scale that is compatible with RS districts. The districts are intended to be applied in areas characterized by a mix of housing types. The districts are also intended to provide a gradual transition between RS districts and higher density RM districts. The RT districts are differentiated primarily on the basis of allowed density (minimum lot area per unit) and floor area ratios.

## 6247 N Rockwell St — Can You Build a Duplex?

**Short answer: No, not by right.** This parcel is zoned **RS-2** (Residential Single-Unit), confirmed via Cook County Address Points (PIN 13012120030000). RS-2 is designed exclusively for detached houses [1], and a two-flat (duplex) is **not a permitted use** in RS-2 [3].

---

### Why the lot math makes it even harder

The lot is 4,125 sq ft (per the Assessor). RS-2 requires a minimum of **5,000 sq ft per dwelling unit** from the zoning table. The calculation: 4,125 ÷ 5,000 = 0.8 → **0 additional units supported by lot area alone** (our calculation). Even if the zoning were upgraded, the lot as-is would not support two units under standard density rules.

---

### What's on the site now

The Assessor records a 1-story, 1,661 sq ft masonry home built in 1925 — a single-family house with 3 bedrooms, 1 full bath, a full basement, and a 1-car garage.

---

### Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU)?

Also **not available here**. Coach houses and conversion units are permitted in RS districts only inside a designated ADU-Allowed RS Area [4]; this parcel is not in one (our calculation per §17-7-0570).

---

### Could you rezone?

Possibly, but it would require a **map amendment** — a discretionary approval requiring aldermanic notice and City Council action [1]. Even if rezoned to RS-3, a two-flat requires the block-face test: a two-flat is only compelled (or lot-area reduced to 1,500 sq ft) in RS-3 when more than 50% of lots on the same block face are already improved with multi-unit buildings [5]. If rezoned to an **RT district**, two-flats are permitted by right [3], subject to bulk and density standards.

---

### Other notes

- **Flood zone:** FEMA Zone X — minimal flood hazard; flood insurance not required.
- **ARO Zone:** This parcel is in an Affordable Requirements Ordinance zone, so any residential development triggered by zoning relief that meets ARO thresholds could carry affordable unit obligations.
- EPA brownfield data was temporarily unavailable; check directly if environmental due diligence is relevant.

Title 17 — CHICAGO ZONING ORDINANCE
Chapter 17-2 — RESIDENTIAL DISTRICTS
§ 17-2-0300 — Bulk and density standards
(part 3 of 23)

17-2-0303-A Minimum Lot Area per Unit Standards. All development in R districts is subject to the following minimum lot-area-per-unit standards. These standards are not to be interpreted as a guarantee that allowed densities can be achieved on every lot . Other factors, such as off-street parking, height limits, dwelling unit sizes and lot configuration may work to limit density more than these standards.

(*See Sec. 17-17-0304 for rules governing the measurement of lot area per unit .)

17-2-0303-B Exemptions.

1. In the RS3 district the minimum lot area per dwelling unit may be reduced to 1,500 square feet when 60% or more of the zoning lots fronting on the same side of the street between the two nearest intersecting streets have been lawfully improved with buildings containing more than one dwelling unit or when the property is located within the “Predominance of the Block” boundaries as defined by Section 17-7-0591. This exemption will only allow for the establishment of a two-unit building .

2. Ground floor Type A units , except those provided in detached houses , are exempt from inclusion in minimum lot area per dwelling unit calculations, in RS3, RT3.5, and RT4 districts.

Chapter 17-4 — DOWNTOWN DISTRICTS
§ 17-4-0400 — Bulk and density standards
(part 6 of 11)

17-4-0409-A Standards. The total number of efficiency units may not exceed the following standards except as specified in Section 17-4-0409-B:

1. The limits on efficiency units do not apply to elderly housing developments, provided that the Zoning Administrator determines that such developments constitute bona fide elderly housing developments.

2. The limits on efficiency units do not apply to transit-served developments within 660 feet of a CTA or Metra rail station entrance or exit or a CTA bus line corridor roadway segment listed in Table 17-17-0400-B.

3. The limits on efficiency units do not apply to the rehabilitation or reuse of an official Chicago Landmark building or an existing “contributing building” within an official Chicago Landmark district located in a DC-16 or DX-16 District.

17-4-0410-A Amount and Dimensions. ## Zoning: RM-4.5 — Multi-Unit Residential

The lot is **3,191 sq ft** (our calculation). Dividing by the 700 sq ft per-unit minimum:

turn1.answer:
**No — this parcel does not qualify for a density, FAR, or height bonus based on transit proximity.**

The parcel at 368 W Chicago Ave (PIN 17044360170000, matched via Cook County Address Points) is zoned **C2-5** (Motor Vehicle-Related Commercial) [1]. While it is unquestionably transit-served — the Chicago (Brown/Purple Line) station is just 0.12 miles away — transit-based FAR and height bonuses are available **only in dash-3 districts** (e.g., B1-3, B2-3, C1-3, C2-3) under [2], and in D-dash-3 downtown districts under [1]. A C2-**5** district does not qualify.

The parcel *does* receive one meaningful transit benefit: the minimum off-street parking requirement can be reduced by up to **100%** under §17-10-0102-B, so you could build with no required parking at all. But there is no by-right density, FAR, or height bonus here.

If you wanted to pursue a transit-based FAR increase, you would need either:
- A **Type 1 Zoning Map Amendment** to rezone to a dash-3 district, or
- Approval through **Planned Development** procedures (§17-13-0600) [2],

and even then, any project providing the FAR increase through that path that also carries affordable units on-site may access supplemental incentives under [3]. All of that is discretionary — requiring aldermanic notice to Ward 27 Ald. Walter R. Burnett (§17-13-0300).

One additional note: the Municipal Code text used here is current through the Council Journal of June 17, 2026. City Council passed 10 Zoning Ordinance amendments after that date, including **SO2026-0025391** (passed October 14, 2026), which added a new Section 17-3-0600 regarding "transient-oriented development (TOD) streets." That amendment is not yet in the published code text, so if Chicago Ave has been designated a TOD street under that ordinance, it could affect what's available here — confirm with the Office of the Zoning Administrator.

CHICAGO MUNICIPAL CODE
Title 2 — CITY GOVERNMENT AND ADMINISTRATION
Chapter 2-120 — COMMISSIONERS AND COMMISSIONS
Article XVII — COMMISSION ON CHICAGO HISTORICAL AND ARCHITECTURAL LANDMARKS (2-120-580 et seq.)
§ 2-120-825 — Permits for demolition of landmarks – City council approval required
(part 1 of 3)

(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this ordinance to the contrary, except as provided in subsection (c), in the case of any permit application for the demolition of 40 percent or more of any building or other structure designated as a "Chicago Landmark" or located in any district designated as a "Chicago Landmark", the commission's decision approving an application issued under Section 2-120-770, Section 2-120-790 or Section 2-120-800 shall be subject to review by the city council. Upon issuing its decision approving an application, the commission shall forward a recommendation for the approval of the permit application, in writing, to the committee on zoning, landmarks and building standards of the city council. Within 75 days after the receipt of the commission's recommendation, the committee on zoning, landmarks and building standards shall consider the commission's recommendation and vote to recommend that the city council accept or reject the commission's recommendation. At the next regular meeting of the city council following the committee's vote, unless the matter is deferred and published in accordance with state law, the city council shall, by passage of an appropriate order, accept or reject the commission's recommendation. If the matter is deferred and published, the city council shall, by passage of an appropriate order, accept or reject the commission's recommendation at the next regular meeting of the city council following the meeting at which the matter was deferred and published. If the city council does not accept or reject the commission's recommendation within the time specified herein, the commission's recommendation shall be deemed to be accepted. The city council's decision shall be based on whether the proposed demolition will adversely affect any significant historical or architectural feature of the improvement or the district, and is in accord with the Standards for Rehabilitation set forth by the United States Secretary of the Interior at 36 C.F.R. 67, as amended from time to time, as well as the criteria to review demolitions as set forth in the Rules and Regulations of the commission.

CHICAGO MUNICIPAL CODE
Title 2 — CITY GOVERNMENT AND ADMINISTRATION
Chapter 2-120 — COMMISSIONERS AND COMMISSIONS
Article XVII — COMMISSION ON CHICAGO HISTORICAL AND ARCHITECTURAL LANDMARKS (2-120-580 et seq.)
§ 2-120-740 — Alteration, relocation or demolition of landmarks – Permit review requirements

No permit for alteration, construction, reconstruction, erection, demolition, relocation, or other work, shall be issued to any applicant by any department of the City of Chicago without the written approval of the commission for any area, place, building, structure, work of art or other object for which the commission has made a preliminary recommendation for landmark status or which has been designated as a "Chicago Landmark" in the following instances: (1) where such permit would allow the alteration or reconstruction of or addition to any improvement which constitutes all or a part of a landmark or proposed landmark; or (2) where such permit would allow the demolition of any improvement which constitutes all or a part of a landmark or proposed landmark; or (3) where a permit would allow the construction or erection of any addition to any improvement or the erection of any new structure or improvement on any land within a landmark district; or (4) where a permit would allow the construction or erection of any sign or billboard within the public view which may be placed on, in, or immediately adjacent to any improvement which constitutes all or part of any landmark or proposed landmark. Any city department which receives an application for a permit as defined in this section shall forward the application, including copies of all detailed plans, designs, elevations, specifications, and documents relating thereto, to the commission within seven days of receipt thereof. It shall be a violation of this ordinance for an owner to perform, authorize or allow work or other acts requiring review without a permit.

Legislative history: (Prior code § 21-77; Added Coun. J. 3-11-87, p. 40272; Amend Coun. J. 2-26-97, p. 40085)

§ 14A-4-407 — DEMOLITION
(part 7 of 8)

If a building or structure is color coded orange or red in the Chicago Historic Resources Survey published in 1996, a demolition permit may not be issued for a period not to exceed 90 days in order to enable the Department of Planning and Development to explore options to preserve the building or structure , including, but not limited to, possible designation of the building or structure as a Chicago Landmark in accordance with Article XVII of Chapter 2-120 of the Municipal Code .

14A-4-407.6.1 Time period.

The 90-day period begins on the date that a copy of the complete demolition permit application, along with one or more photographs accurately depicting the current condition of the building or structure identified in that application, is submitted by the applicant to the Historic Preservation Division of the Department of Planning and Development.

14A-4-407.6.2 Extension.

The 90-day period may be extended for any additional period by mutual written agreement between the applicant and the Department of Planning and Development.

## Demolition at 1601 N Milwaukee Ave — Short Answer: **Yes, but with significant hurdles**

The parcel (PIN 14313320180000, matched via Cook County Address Points) is zoned **B3-2** and is not itself a designated Chicago Landmark building — but it sits inside the **Milwaukee Avenue District (HD-56)**, an official Chicago Landmark district. That single fact is the dominant constraint on demolition.

---

### 1. Chicago Landmark District Review — Required Before Any Permit

Because this address is within Milwaukee Avenue District (HD-56), no demolition permit can be issued without the **Commission on Chicago Landmarks' prior written approval** [2]. The Commission reviews whether the proposed work adversely affects any significant historical or architectural feature of the district, applying the U.S. Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation (36 C.F.R. 67) [1]. If the Commission approves demolition of 40% or more of the structure, that decision is then subject to review by the **City Council's Committee on Zoning, Landmarks and Building Standards**, which has 75 days to act before the Commission's recommendation is deemed accepted [1].

This landmark-district review is **not** a rubber stamp — it is a substantive preservation process and can result in denial.

### 2. CHRS Orange Rating — 90-Day Hold

The building is rated **"orange"** in the 1996 Chicago Historic Resources Survey under the name *Noel State Bank*. Under [3], a demolition permit for an orange-coded building **may not be issued for up to 90 days** after a complete application and photographs are submitted to the Historic Preservation Division of the Department of Planning and Development. That window exists specifically to allow the City to explore preservation options, including potential landmark designation. The 90-day period can be extended by mutual written agreement [3].

This hold runs *in addition to* (not instead of) the landmark-district Commission review above.

### 3. If Demolition Is Approved — What Comes Next?

If you ultimately clear both reviews, the base zoning (B3-2, §17-3-0104) would govern any replacement development:

- **FAR:** 2.2 | **Max height:** 45–50 ft | **Min lot area per unit:** 1,000 sq ft
- The ~11,951 sq ft lot (our calculation) supports up to **11 dwelling units** by lot area alone (11,951 ÷ 1,000 = 11 units), though FAR, height, and parking standards also apply
- **Parking:** As a transit-served parcel, minimum parking can be reduced by up to 100% under §17-10-0102-B — but B3-2 is not a dash-3 district, so no FAR or height density bonus applies by right
- Any new construction within the landmark district still requires Commission approval [2]

### 4. One Post-June 2026 Amendment Worth Noting

City Council passed **SO2026-0027187** on September 23, 2026 — after the Municipal Code text this analysis relies on (current through the Council Journal of June 17, 2026) — titled "exempting adaptive reuse or rehabilitated strip centers from prohibitions within Milwaukee Avenue Special Character Overlay District." That ordinance is not yet in the published code, so I cannot say how it applies here; its relevance would depend on the specific scope of the overlay and the work proposed. How to verify: check the City Clerk record for SO2026-0027187.

---

### Summary of Steps Required

| Step | Authority |
|---|---|
| Commission on Chicago Landmarks written approval | [2] |
| 90-day CHRS orange hold (Historic Preservation Division) | [3] |
| City Council review if demolition ≥ 40% of structure | [1] |
| New construction in district also needs Commission approval | [2] |

**How to verify zoning:** Chicago Zoning Map at https://gisapps.chicago.gov/ZoningMapWeb/?liab=1&config=zoning | For a binding determination, a Zoning Verification Letter costs $150 and takes up to 30 days through the Office of the Zoning Administrator.
